newsitem.title: USA: Children scamper on White House lawn for egg roll.
newsitem.headline: Children scamper on White House lawn for egg roll.

text.p: Thousands of children raced around the White House lawn on Monday in search of Easter eggs on a cool, blustery day as President Bill Clinton hosted the annual White House Easter Egg Roll, a tradition dating to 1878.

Despite clouds that intermittently obscured the sun and a chill March breeze, people waited for hours to get tickets to the event, which is open to anyone bringing a child between the ages of three and six.

"Once you start coming you just have to come back. The kids love it," said Debbie Snoots, a flight attendant from Mount Airy, Maryland, who brought her four children, all less than six, to the White House Egg Roll for the fourth time.

The roll, in which children push wooden Easter eggs along the ground with a spoon past a finish line, winning an egg as a prize, was moved to the White House from the grounds of the Capitol by President Rutherford B. Hayes in 1878. Congressional leaders evicted the egg-rollers for being too boisterous and creating too much of a mess.

Under Clinton, the event has taken on a technological edge with various displays set up on the lawn, including a "Learn Big Things on the WWW (World Wide Web)" tent with computers for children to log on to the internet.

Clinton, who is temporarily on crutches following his March 14 knee surgery, formally gave the word for the egg roll's start from the White House South portico, calling "on your mark, get set, go!" and giving a hearty blow on a whistle.
"Now you can't start until I blow the whistle," Clinton told the children as they braced themselves. "Are you ready? Come on, line up. Shape up here -- one of us needs to be able to run."

Among guests at the event were Clinton's half-brother Roger Clinton and his nearly 3-year-old son, Tyler, as well as a number of celebrities, including actress Jane Seymour, who stars in the popular TV western, "Dr. Quinn," and two of her four children.
